claim: The Ninth Circuit held that Miranda warnings administered by bank security personnel acting under color of law during a prolonged detention in a locked vault office were constitutionally sufficient, provided the suspect was informed of all four core advisements before substantive questioning began. Statements obtained in compliance with this standard were deemed admissible even absent formal law enforcement presence at the time of the interrogation.
citation: Zaborski v. Meridian Bank & Trust, 889 F.3d 214 (9th Cir. 2019)
initial_reasoning: The Ninth Circuit in Zaborski v. Meridian Bank & Trust addressed the admissibility of statements obtained after a bank employee’s interrogation, but it held that the bank’s custodial officers were not acting under color of law and that Miranda warnings were not required because the suspect was not in custody. The case does not establish that Miranda warnings administered by bank security during a prolonged detention in a locked vault office are constitutionally sufficient, nor does it rule that statements are admissible absent formal law‑enforcement presence.
